<reason>PRO (Side B) won by progressively narrowing the debate to a single decisive question—who owns the actor's face and voice when the contract is silent—and by using pressure questions to force CON into an honest but damaging admission that a silent contract permits a studio to clone the actor's voice and write new dialogue unpaid. B's reframe that CON had "adopted the motion's mechanism and disputes only the default" was accurate and sharp, and the day-player example made the stakes concrete. CON (Side A) argued rigorously and consistently, landing real points: PRO conceded the harm is tool-independent, and PRO's own "consistent with script and character" clause still requires the same scope interpretation CON relies on. But CON never gave a compelling reason why the default should favor the studio, and its Q&A concession left it defending a position a third-party reader finds hard to accept. B's clipped rebuttal is a minor execution cost; A's earnest but abstract style never generated comparable pressure.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Pressure Q1 ("when a contract is silent... may the studio clone the actor's voice... yes or no?") followed by A's "Yes—for new dialogue within the reasonably understood role," which B then dismantled in closing: the studio decides scope, the actor finds out at the premiere, and her remedy is a lawsuit.</best_rebuttal>
